extracted.intended_audience: in-house IP teams, patent managers, and attorneys selecting or evaluating patent prosecutors / law firms
extracted.subtask_short: evaluating patent prosecutors with TIP Tool
extracted.subtask_description: Step-by-step guidance for using the TIP Tool™ Prosecutor Analysis feature to evaluate and compare patent prosecutors and law firms based on allowance rates, timelines, office-action behavior, RCE patterns, client lists, and other prosecution metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate allowance rates in context
rubrics_metrics.description: See how a prosecutor’s grant rate compares to their examiners and art unit benchmarks, not just in isolation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Core principle: Never judge an allowance rate without comparing it to the examiner and art unit averages. A high allowance rate can reflect either skill or an easy examiner/art unit; compare to examiner averages and GAU averages to interpret meaningfully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecutor identity verification (prosecutor details)
rubrics_metrics.description: Confirm prosecutor identity via name, law firm, license years, office address, phone number, USPTO registration number, and email (where available).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Why it matters: Ensures you have the right person (attorneys share names or move firms). The registration number is useful for cross-referencing USPTO records. This check prevents mistaken attribution of performance data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance Rate — four-layer concentric arc chart and color coding
rubrics_metrics.description: Visualize performance at four levels simultaneously: outer arc = individual prosecutor allowance rate; second arc = prosecutor's average GAU allowance rate; third arc = aggregated examiners' allowance rate; inner arc = aggregated examiners' GAU allowance rate. Color coding indicates performance vs GAU (Red: >10% below GAU, Orange/Yellow: within ±10% of GAU, Green: >10% above GAU).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Why it matters: Shows performance in context rather than as an isolated number. Example: a prosecutor with 88% may actually be above both examiner and GAU benchmarks. Use the chart to distinguish exceptional skill from favorable examiner/art-unit assignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the Prosecutor Profile Table to compare key metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Head-to-head comparison across prosecutor, their Group Art Units, aggregated examiners they worked with, and those examiners' GAUs showing: Total Applications, Granted Patents, Allowance Rate (with performance badges), Abandoned/Rejected Applications, Pending Applications, Average Grant Time, Average Office Actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use-case: Size up a prosecutor’s complete track record at a glance. The tool also generates a plain-English narrative summary tying the numbers together to explain context. Look for consistently better/worse metrics vs GAU/examiners to identify strengths/weaknesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution efficiency — issuance time and average office actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare time-to-issuance (shortest, average, longest) and office actions before issuance (least, average, most) for the prosecutor versus the examiners they worked with; see GAU breakdown showing allowance rate per art unit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Why it matters: Shorter grant times and fewer office action rounds reduce cost and accelerate product timelines. Use this to set expectations and decide if an attorney's speed/efficiency fits your timeline and budget.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze RCE behavior and success rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Track how often the prosecutor’s cases required RCEs (no RCE, 1 RCE, 2 RCEs, 3+ RCEs) and outcomes: percentage abandoned/rejected after RCE, how often first RCE led to immediate notice of allowance, average RCEs per application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Why it matters: RCEs cost time and money. A low RCE rate and high RCE success rate indicate efficient upfront prosecution and fewer wasted cycles. Compare RCE outcomes to understand risk profiles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time between response and office action (turnaround time)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure how quickly the prosecutor typically responds after receiving a rejection (FR and NFR) and compare to examiner response times; show minimum, average, maximum turnaround times and related stats (e.g., percent of cases granted without any Final Rejection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Why it matters: Helps set internal timelines and stakeholder expectations. Use these metrics to answer 'when can we expect to hear back?' and to manage scheduling during prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance trend (year-over-year performance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Yearly bar charts showing Granted (green), Abandoned (red), and Pending (blue) cases; toggles to display Filing Year vs Grant Year and case Value vs Percentage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Why it matters: Detect whether performance is improving, declining, or stable over time. Tip: Switch to Grant Year to see recent issued patents; use Filing Year to assess lifecycle outcomes for a cohort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office action patterns — prosecutor vs Group Art Unit
rubrics_metrics.description: Side-by-side charts comparing percentages of applications that received No Office Action, Non-Final Rejection (NFR), or Final Rejection (FR) for the prosecutor and the GAU; ability to drill down on number of NFR rounds (1, 2, 3+).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Why it matters: Reveals prosecution difficulty in context. A lower Final Rejection rate vs GAU (e.g., 17.4% vs 30.9%) signals meaningful advantage. Drilling into NFR rounds distinguishes single-shot resolutions vs protracted back-and-forth prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office actions trend (distribution of total office actions in granted cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pie-chart breakdown of how many total office actions (Final + Non-Final) were involved in the prosecutor’s granted cases: No Office Action, 1 Office Action, 2 Office Actions, 3+ Office Actions, plus average days to allowance per track.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Why it matters: High proportion of grants with zero or one office action suggests well-drafted applications and lower costs. Use the distribution and timing to estimate expected prosecution cycles and costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popular applicants and conflict checking
rubrics_metrics.description: List and charts showing companies/applicants the prosecutor has represented most frequently, including per-applicant case volumes and allowance rates; summary stats for top applicants and highest-volume applicant allowance rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Why it matters: Reveals prosecutor's client mix (big-company portfolios vs startups) and serves as a conflict check. Tip: Look for overlap with competitors or adjacent-space companies; even absent a formal conflict, deep ties to a competitor may be undesirable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benchmark comparisons are essential (interpretation guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Always compare prosecutor metrics to examiner and art unit benchmarks; a number without context can mislead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated guidance: Use the concentric arc chart and GAU/examiner comparisons to interpret allowance rates and other metrics. The data should prompt better questions, not serve as a final verdict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for case complexity and assignment bias (lower stats ≠ poor performance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lower allowance rates or longer times may reflect attorneys taking harder cases, contested claims, or difficult examiners rather than poor skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Why it matters: Use qualitative follow-up (type of technology, claim scope, examiner difficulty) when interpreting lower-performance metrics. Don’t automatically penalize attorneys working on high-complexity matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volume/sample-size considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: An attorney with very few cases in your area may not have enough data to draw reliable conclusions; look for meaningful sample sizes before committing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Why it matters: Small sample sizes produce noisy, unreliable metrics. Use Advanced Search filters to ensure you're viewing a sufficiently large and relevant dataset (e.g., by GAU, time window, or client).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recent activity as a signal of current capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Someone with a strong historical record but little recent activity may not be actively taking new work; use filters to focus on recent filings and current caseloads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Why it matters: Recent filings indicate ongoing practice and availability. A historically strong but inactive prosecutor may not be a good choice for new matters; prefer candidates with relevant recent experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use plain-English narrative summaries to interpret numeric data
rubrics_metrics.description: Below tables the tool generates a plain-English narrative tying numbers together and explaining how prosecutor performance relates to examiners and GAU context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Why it matters: Narrative summaries help non-technical stakeholders understand implications of the metrics and can surface the most salient comparative insights quickly.
